# Assumptions

1. No limit on the number of columns  
2. The columns being compared are numbers, no other requirements  
3. The join conditions are AND-ed together

# Overall algorithm

1. ~~Build ranges~~ Not doing because it will be hard to detect these in real join queries  
   1. ~~Detect impossible conditions \[element\>a and element\<a\] \[immediately return a table with 0 rows\] Not going to implement because this is unlikely to be part of a query~~  
   2. ~~Remove subranges~~

1. For each condition  
   1. Sort just the smaller column. Comparison between sorting options below (where l is the size of the larger column and s is the size of the smaller column):

| Step | Sort Smaller column S | Sort Larger Column L | Sort both |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Sort column | O(s\*log(s)) | O(l\*log(l)) | O(s\*log(s))+O(l\*log(l)) |
| Iterate through the other column. This will have to be done when evaluating the query | O(l\*log(s)) | O(s\*log(l)) | O(s\*log(l-alreadyUsedSpots)) |

![][image1]![][image2]

After looking at the images above and doing Big O analysis, I decided to sort just the smaller column.

To summarize, step 1 is to sort column the smaller column S in each condition. Optimization opportunity: do not sort the same column multiple times.
